claims.claim: Didymus the Blind was an Egyptian theologian and monk who lived approximately 313–398 AD.
Didymus became blind in early childhood, before he had learned to read.
Athanasius appointed Didymus head of the school at Alexandria, where he taught for about half a century.
Didymus remained a layman all his life.
Didymus was heavily influenced by Origen and was a loyal follower of his teachings.
Because of this condemnation, most of Didymus's works were not copied during the Middle Ages and were subsequently lost.
The Commentary on the Octateuch and the Books of Kingdoms was previously known only through fragments in catena manuscripts and extracts cited by Procopius of Gaza before the 1941 discovery.

In 1941, British military engineers discovered a hoard of at least eight papyrus codices in a subterranean cavern at Tura, about 10 miles outside Cairo, containing previously lost biblical commentaries by Didymus.
The Tura papyri contain Didymus's commentaries on Genesis, Ecclesiastes, Job, Zechariah, and Psalms 20–46, which had been assumed to be no longer extant.

The Commentary on Genesis from the Tura find may have been Didymus's earliest work, based on his silence regarding his other works, less frequent remarks on specific heresies and Christological interpretations, and heavier reliance on Philo and Origen.
